artiest/jimmy-garrison.text:
Jimmy Garrison was an American jazz double bassist, best known for his work with John Coltrane from 1961 to 1967. He was born in Miami in 1934 and moved to Philadelphia at the age of ten, where he learned to play bass in his final year of school. He grew up in that city's jazz scene of the 1950s, among bassists such as Reggie Workman and Henry Grimes, pianist McCoy Tyner and trumpeter Lee Morgan. For a short time he played in a trio that Bill Evans had started.

In 1962 he formally became a member of Coltrane's quartet, succeeding Workman. One of his first recordings with Coltrane and drummer Elvin Jones was the long blues trio Chasin' the Trane. He played on many Coltrane records, including A Love Supreme. In the 1960s he also worked with Ornette Coleman, beginning in 1961 on Ornette on Tenor. After Coltrane's death he played with Alice Coltrane, Hampton Hawes, Archie Shepp and groups led by Elvin Jones. In 1971 and 1972 he taught at Wesleyan University and Bennington College.

His playing was innovative and melodic. He often played with broken time and avoided the steady quarter notes of a walking bass, so that he suggested the pulse rather than played it. He used double stops, sometimes struck the strings with his thumb, and often played unaccompanied solos. He died of lung cancer in 1976.
artiest/jimmy-garrison.listen: Listen to A Love Supreme by John Coltrane and notice the bass: it keeps repeating and carries the piece, while the saxophone and drums move freely around it.

artiest/jimmy-giuffre.text:
Jimmy Giuffre was an American clarinettist, saxophonist, composer and arranger, born in Dallas in 1921. He studied in Texas and became known as an arranger for Woody Herman's big band, for which he wrote Four Brothers in 1947. Later he developed forms of jazz in which the players could interact freely, anticipating free improvisation.

His first trio consisted of Giuffre, guitarist Jim Hall and bassist Ralph Peña, later Jim Atlas. He called their style blues-based folk jazz. In 1957 he had a small hit when The Train and the River was featured on the television programme The Sound of Jazz. He then replaced the bassist with valve trombonist Bob Brookmeyer. That trio can be seen in the film Jazz on a Summer's Day, shot at the 1958 Newport Jazz Festival.

In 1961 he formed a new trio with pianist Paul Bley and bassist Steve Swallow. Giuffre now concentrated on the clarinet. The trio received little attention at the time, but critics later called it one of the most important groups in jazz. It played free jazz in a quiet, concentrated way, not aggressively like Albert Ayler or Archie Shepp. On their last record, Free Fall from 1963, the music consisted entirely of improvisation, years before the wave of free improvisation in Europe. Giuffre later taught in New York and Boston, among other places, and died in 2008.
artiest/jimmy-giuffre.listen: Listen to The Train and the River and notice how chamber music and folk gently come together: clarinet, guitar and bass keep each other in balance without drums.

artiest/jimmy-jam.text:
Jimmy Jam, born James Harris III, is an American producer, songwriter and keyboardist, born in Minneapolis in 1959. He is the son of the blues and jazz musician Cornbread Harris. Through a study programme at the University of Minnesota he met Terry Lewis, with whom he would work throughout his career. In the mid-1970s he played in Mind & Matter, an eleven-piece band.

Jam ended up in Flyte Tyme, Lewis's band, which Prince remodelled into The Time in 1981. Alongside their band work, Jam and Lewis began producing for other artists. When a snowstorm in Atlanta made them miss a gig, because they had secretly been in the studio there working for the S.O.S. Band, Prince fired them. But the song from that session, Just Be Good to Me, became a hit and made their name. They went on to produce Cherrelle and Alexander O'Neal, among others, and in 1986 Janet Jackson's album Control, followed by Rhythm Nation 1814 (1989).

Within the duo, Jimmy Jam is above all the man behind the keyboards and the machines. Their productions revolved around the Roland TR-808 drum machine, tight synthesizer lines and funk grooves, the sound that became known as the Minneapolis sound. Jam later also became chairman of the American academy that presents the Grammys. In 2022 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Lewis.
artiest/jimmy-jam.listen: Listen to When I Think of You (1986) by Janet Jackson. Notice the tight drum machine and the short, funky synthesizer chords that give the song its spring.

artiest/jimmy-jam-en-terry-lewis.text:
Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis are an American duo of producers and songwriters from Minneapolis. Jimmy Jam, born James Harris III, was born in 1959, Terry Lewis in 1956. They met during a study programme at the University of Minnesota. Lewis played in the band Flyte Tyme, which Jam later joined. In 1981 Prince remodelled that group into The Time, in which the duo played the instruments.

Meanwhile they also produced for others. They made Just Be Good to Me for the S.O.S. Band in Atlanta, but because a snowstorm kept them there, they missed a concert by The Time. Prince fired them, but the song became a hit. They went on to work with Cherrelle, Alexander O'Neal and others. In 1986 they produced Control, Janet Jackson's breakthrough album, for which they received a Grammy. Rhythm Nation 1814 (1989) was even more successful, and they continued to work with her later, on albums such as The Velvet Rope. In 1991 they started their own label, Perspective Records.

The sound of Jam and Lewis was tight and electronic, built on the Roland TR-808 drum machine, with synthesizers and funk rhythms. This became the Minneapolis sound, which they took from Prince and developed further. They wrote dozens of hits for artists ranging from Michael Jackson to Mariah Carey and Boyz II Men, and in doing so helped define the R&B of the 1980s and 1990s. In 2022 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/jimmy-jam-en-terry-lewis.listen: Listen to Nasty (1986) by Janet Jackson. Notice the hard, dry hits of the drum machine and the short synthesizer stabs, and how Jackson's voice cuts fiercely over the top.

artiest/jimmy-lyons.text:
Jimmy Lyons was an American alto saxophonist, born in Jersey City in 1931 and raised in Harlem and the Bronx. He got his first saxophone in the mid-1940s and took lessons with Buster Bailey. After school he was drafted into the army and served 21 months as an infantryman in Korea. He then played for a year in army bands, studied at New York University and, in the late 1950s, worked for the United States Postal Service to pay for his music.

In 1960 he succeeded Archie Shepp as saxophonist in the Cecil Taylor Unit. From the sessions at the Café Montmartre in 1962 onwards, his sound was a defining part of the group. From the mid-1960s he was the only permanent member, until his death. Taylor never worked as often with any other musician. Lyons played in a style that grew out of Charlie Parker and kept Taylor's avant-garde music connected to the jazz tradition, with a strong melodic sense.

In the 1970s he also led his own group with bassoonist Karen Borca and drummer Paul Murphy. It often performed on the loft jazz scene around Studio Rivbea. In 1976 he took part in A Rat's Mass, a theatre production directed by Taylor. Lyons died of lung cancer in 1986. He made few records under his own name. Ayler Records later released a five-CD box set of recordings from 1972 to 1985.
artiest/jimmy-lyons.listen: Listen to a recording by the Cecil Taylor Unit and notice Lyons's alto saxophone: between Taylor's wild piano sounds, his melody rings out remarkably clear and bluesy.

artiest/jimmy-mcpartland.text:
Jimmy McPartland was an American cornettist, born in Chicago in 1907. His father was a music teacher and baseball player. He grew up partly in children's homes and got into trouble with the law. By his own account, music saved him: he took up the violin at the age of five and the cornet at fifteen.

In the 1920s he played in the Austin High School Gang, together with Bud Freeman, Frank Teschemacher, his brother Dick, Joe Sullivan and Dave Tough, among others. The group learned from records they heard in the sweet shop Spoon and Straw and tried to play them note for note. They helped shape the Chicago style: lively, full of improvisation and inspired by New Orleans. In 1924 he went to New York to take Bix Beiderbecke's place in the Wolverines. Beiderbecke became his friend and chose for him the cornet that he played throughout his career. In 1927 he took part in a recording session by McKenzie and Condon's Chicagoans, with China Boy and Nobody's Sweetheart. He then played with Ben Pollack for two years.

Later he worked with Eddie Condon, Art Hodes, Gene Krupa, Benny Goodman, Jack Teagarden and Tommy Dorsey, and often led his own band. He was married to the pianist Marian McPartland. His career spanned more than fifty years. He also contributed to the Dixieland revival of the 1940s and 1950s.
artiest/jimmy-mcpartland.listen: Listen to China Boy by McKenzie and Condon's Chicagoans from 1927 and notice the lively interplay, in which the horns play across one another instead of neatly taking turns.

artiest/jimmy-page.text:
Jimmy Page is an English guitarist and producer, born in 1944 in Heston, a suburb of London. At the age of twelve he found a guitar in the house in Epsom where his family had come to live. He taught himself to play, mostly by listening to records. Baby Let's Play House by Elvis Presley, with guitarist Scotty Moore, was the decisive moment. He also listened to skiffle, folk and blues guitarists such as Elmore James, B.B. King and Otis Rush.

In the early 1960s Page became one of London's busiest session guitarists. He sometimes played three sessions a day, for The Kinks, on the B-side of The Who's first single, for Them and on Shirley Bassey's Goldfinger, among others. He also worked as a producer for the label Immediate. In 1966 he joined The Yardbirds, and when that group split up in 1968, he founded Led Zeppelin in London, with singer Robert Plant, bassist and keyboardist John Paul Jones and drummer John Bonham. Page wrote and produced the band's music, with songs such as Whole Lotta Love (1969) and Stairway to Heaven (1971). After Bonham's death in 1980 he played in The Firm and with David Coverdale and Robert Plant, among others.

Page combined blues and rock with folk and Eastern influences. His strength lay in heavy, simple riffs that carry an entire song, and in his work as a producer, with which he shaped the band's sound. He is counted among the most influential guitarists ever, and his way of playing became a model for hard rock and heavy metal.
artiest/jimmy-page.listen: Listen to Whole Lotta Love (1969) by Led Zeppelin. Notice the short, heavy guitar riff that keeps coming back and carries the whole song.

artiest/jimmy-rushing.text:
Jimmy Rushing was an American singer and pianist from Oklahoma City, born in 1901. He came from a musical family: his father played trumpet, and his mother and her brother sang. He studied music theory at high school and, which was unusual at the time, went on to Wilberforce University. His first performance as a singer was in 1924, when a singer in a club invited him to sing something. In the early 1920s he toured the Midwest and California as an itinerant bluesman, and played and sang in Los Angeles with Jelly Roll Morton.

In 1927 he joined Walter Page's Blue Devils and in 1929 the band of Bennie Moten. After Moten's death in 1935 he stayed with the orchestra that Count Basie took over. He was its singer for thirteen years, until 1948. He sang in the Kansas City jump blues style, for example in Sent for You Yesterday and Boogie Woogie. He was known as Mister Five by Five, after his build, and a song with that title became a hit for Harry James in 1942.

Rushing was a powerful singer with a range from baritone to tenor. His voice could rise above the horns of a big band. Basie said that as a blues vocalist he had never had an equal, although Rushing really saw himself as a ballad singer. After Basie he carried on with his own groups and worked with Duke Ellington and Dave Brubeck. In 1957 he sang I Left My Baby on the television programme The Sound of Jazz. He died in 1972.
artiest/jimmy-rushing.listen: Listen to Sent for You Yesterday with Count Basie's orchestra and notice how Rushing's voice rises above the horns without ever seeming to strain.

artiest/jimmy-smith.text: Jimmy Smith, from Norristown near Philadelphia, began as a pianist and switched to the Hammond B-3 organ in the early 1950s. He practised for months on end and played the bass lines with his feet on the pedals and with his left hand. Alfred Lion of Blue Note heard him in 1956 and signed him on the spot. Smith played bebop and blues on the organ with the speed of a saxophonist and used the rotating Leslie speaker for a floating sound. The Sermon! (1958) is a long, relaxed blues. Later he made big band albums for Verve. Smith became the model for almost all later jazz organists.
artiest/jimmy-smith.listen: Listen to the organ: bass, chords and a fast melody all at once, played by a single musician.

artiest/jimmy-somerville.text:
Jimmy Somerville is a Scottish singer, born in 1961 and raised in Ruchill, a district in the north of Glasgow. In 1980 he moved to London, where he lived in squats and immersed himself in the city's gay culture. He attended the London Gay Teenage Group, a meeting place for young gay people.

In 1983 Somerville founded the synth-pop group Bronski Beat. After only nine gigs the trio were given a record contract. The first single, Smalltown Boy (1984), is about a gay boy who is rejected by his family and flees his home town, a story that resembled Somerville's own. It became a big hit, in the Netherlands too. The album The Age of Consent (1984) showed on its inner sleeve how the legal age of consent for sex between men differed from country to country. In 1985 Somerville left and, with pianist Richard Coles, started The Communards. Their version of Don't Leave Me This Way became the best-selling single of 1986 in Britain. He then continued as a solo artist, with Read My Lips (1989) and covers such as Sylvester's You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real).

Somerville stands out for his high, powerful falsetto, which floats above the electronic beats. He was one of the first pop stars to be openly gay and to sing about it. In doing so, in the 1980s, the time of AIDS and prejudice, he gave a voice to a group that was rarely heard in pop music.
artiest/jimmy-somerville.listen: Listen to Smalltown Boy (1984) by Bronski Beat. Notice the contrast between the cool, pulsing synthesizers and Somerville's high, vulnerable falsetto.

artiest/jinsang.text:
Jinsang is a lo-fi hip hop producer, also known as chillhop. It is a stage name, used, among other things, for instrumental beats that became popular as background music for studying and relaxing. The source available was about a Korean classical pianist with a similar name, who is not meant here. Little is therefore recorded here about the person behind the project, and the text confines itself to what is known.

Jinsang's music follows the familiar lo-fi style. A slow hip hop rhythm from a drum machine is combined with soft jazz chords, often a piano or electric piano, and a warm, deliberately imperfect sound with crackling vinyl noise. The tracks are instrumental and usually short, so that they loop well. Such a beat recalls the samples of J Dilla and Nujabes, who defined the style.

Affection from 2016 belongs to this repertoire. Lo-fi hip hop grew in those years mainly on the internet, through video channels and streaming services, where the music was shared without vocals and without a clear star. The genre shows how a small, intimate production made with simple means can reach a large worldwide audience, and how popular music can also serve as atmosphere and background.
artiest/jinsang.listen: Listen to Affection and notice the drum machine and the soft chords: can you hear the crackle of the vinyl noise, and does the rhythm sound deliberately a little loose and uneven?

artiest/jo-jones.text:
Jo Jones was an American jazz drummer, born in Chicago in 1911. He grew up in Alabama, where he learned several instruments, including saxophone, piano and drums. He worked as a drummer and tap dancer in carnival shows and, in the late 1920s, joined Walter Page's Blue Devils in Oklahoma City. In 1931 he recorded with trumpeter Lloyd Hunter's orchestra and in 1934 he joined Count Basie's band. From 1934 to 1948 he formed the rhythm section of the Count Basie Orchestra. To distinguish him from the younger drummer Philly Joe Jones, he later became known as Papa Jo Jones.

His playing changed the role of the drums. He was one of the first to promote the use of brushes and he shifted the timekeeping from the bass drum to the hi-hat. This differed from the prevailing style of Gene Krupa, who loudly hit the bass drum on every beat. Jones often left the bass drum out altogether and kept the hi-hat constantly opening and closing. This gave the rhythm a light, continuous sway that later drummers adopted.

He influenced Buddy Rich, Kenny Clarke, Roy Haynes, Max Roach and Louie Bellson. He appeared in films, including the 1944 music film Jammin' the Blues. In 1979 he was inducted into the Alabama Jazz Hall of Fame and in 1985 he received an American Jazz Masters fellowship. His memoir, Rifftide, appeared in 2011. He died in 1985.
artiest/jo-jones.listen: Listen to a recording by the Count Basie Orchestra from the 1930s and notice the drums: the hi-hat ticks lightly and continuously and the bass drum does not play on every beat.

artiest/jo-stafford.text:
Jo Stafford was an American traditional pop singer, born in Coalinga, California, in 1917. Her career spanned five decades, from the late 1930s to the early 1980s. She trained as a classical singer to become an opera singer, but chose popular music. Her pure voice was widely praised. With her two older sisters she formed the Stafford Sisters, who worked on radio and in films. In 1936 they made their first record with Louis Prima.

In 1938 she formed the vocal group The Pied Pipers with others. Paul Weston, an arranger for Tommy Dorsey, brought the group into Dorsey's orchestra, where she also sang solos. When Frank Sinatra joined Dorsey, they often sang together. Their version of I'll Never Smile Again topped the Billboard chart for twelve weeks in 1940. In 1944 Stafford left Dorsey and recorded many songs that are now standards, for Capitol and Columbia, often with Paul Weston's orchestra. She also sang duets with Gordon MacRae and Frankie Laine.

In 1952 she married Weston. Together they invented the comic duo Jonathan and Darlene Edwards, an incompetent lounge act that parodied well-known songs and drew a large audience. According to the source, up to 1955 she had sold more records worldwide than any other female singer. She died in 2008. Stafford's importance lies in her pure, unaffected voice and the vocal group work of the swing era, which later carried over into pop music.
artiest/jo-stafford.listen: Listen to I'll Never Smile Again by Tommy Dorsey, the Pied Pipers and Frank Sinatra and notice how the solo voice and the group singing alternate.

artiest/jo-yeong-wook.text: Jo Yeong-wook (born in 1962) is the regular musical partner of director Park Chan-wook. For Oldboy (2003) he worked with a small team of composers. The music is strikingly classical in form: waltzes and string pieces that give the violence on screen a tragic, almost operatic charge. Most of the cues are named after old films, often films noirs. For the vampire film Bakjwi (2009) he won the Blue Dragon Award for best film music, and for Ah-ga-ssi (2016) he wrote an elegant, European-sounding score for a story set in Korea under Japanese rule. He shows how Korean cinema uses Western classical forms.
artiest/jo-yeong-wook.listen: In The Last Waltz, listen for the three-beat rhythm and the contrast between the elegant waltz and the tension in the film.

artiest/joan-baez.text:
Joan Baez is an American singer, singer-songwriter and activist, born on Staten Island in 1941. Her father was originally from Mexico, worked for UNESCO and had the family move often, including to Europe and the Middle East. The family became Quakers, a tradition she still counts herself part of. After high school she moved to Boston, where she performed in the Cambridge folk scene. In 1959 she recorded an album with two others that was released as Folksingers Round Harvard Square.

Her real career began at the first Newport Folk Festival in 1959. In 1960 came her first album for Vanguard, Joan Baez, which was recorded in four days. Her first three albums went gold. She also wrote songs herself, but sang mostly traditional songs and the work of others, such as There but for Fortune by Phil Ochs and The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down by The Band. She also recorded Farewell, Angelina, Forever Young, Joe Hill, Here's to You and We Shall Overcome. Diamonds and Rust appeared in 1975.

Her music is protest music and is about social justice, a cause she calls the core of her life. She campaigned for civil rights and non-violence. In 1969 she sang fourteen songs at Woodstock. Later she broadened her style with folk rock, pop, country and gospel. She has been performing for more than sixty years and has made more than thirty albums. Baez gave the folk movement of the 1960s a pure, clear voice.
artiest/joan-baez.listen: Listen to Diamonds and Rust and notice how her clear soprano and the acoustic guitar tell a personal, almost spoken story.

artiest/joan-jett.text:
Joan Jett, born Joan Marie Larkin in 1958 near Philadelphia, is an American singer, guitarist and songwriter. She got her first guitar at thirteen and stopped taking lessons because the teacher wanted to teach her folk. After a move to California she co-founded the Runaways at sixteen, together with drummer Sandy West. With band members such as Lita Ford, Cherie Currie and Jackie Fox, the group released four studio albums between 1975 and 1979. They were the support act for Cheap Trick, the Ramones and Van Halen, among others. In Japan, Europe and Asia they were more popular than in the United States.

After the break-up Jett went solo. Record companies rejected her work, so with producer Kenny Laguna she founded her own label, Blackheart Records. Her debut album appeared in 1980. She then formed Joan Jett and the Blackhearts. Their 1981 album I Love Rock 'n Roll reached number two on the American album chart. The title song, a cover of the Arrows, topped the Hot 100 and became her trademark. I Hate Myself for Loving You followed in 1988, along with other hits. She also produced the only studio album by the Germs.

Jett is called the Godmother of Punk. In 1987 she starred alongside Michael J. Fox in the film Light of Day, and in 2015 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the Blackhearts. Her importance lies in her sturdy, simple guitar sound and in the fact that, as a woman, she ran her own label and band.
artiest/joan-jett.listen: Listen to I Love Rock 'n Roll and notice how little is needed: a sturdy guitar riff, a pounding rhythm and a chorus you can sing along to straight away.

artiest/joanne-catherall.text:
Joanne Catherall is an English singer and one of the two female vocalists of the synth-pop band The Human League. She was born in 1962. In 1980, when she had just turned eighteen and was still at school, she and her best friend Susan Ann Sulley were discovered in the Crazy Daisy Nightclub in Sheffield by Philip Oakey, the group's singer.

The Human League had just split up acrimoniously. Only Oakey and Adrian Wright remained, while the group had to start a European tour within a week. Oakey quickly looked for new members and asked the two girls, who had never sung or danced professionally. Their parents gave permission only after Oakey had visited them in person. On that tour they were at first dancers with small singing parts, for thirty pounds a week. The audience was hostile, because fans had bought tickets for the old all-male line-up. In December 1980 both women became full members.

In 1981 the group broke through with producer Martin Rushent. Sound of the Crowd was a top twenty hit and the first single with vocals from both women. Love Action and Open Your Heart followed in the top ten, and in October the album Dare. Catherall became known for her black kohl and bright red lipstick. The single Don't You Want Me got an expensive video, with a duet by Oakey and Sulley and backing vocals from Catherall. She is still a member and shares the band's company with Oakey and Sulley.
artiest/joanne-catherall.listen: Listen to Don't You Want Me by The Human League and notice the three singers: Oakey and Sulley sing against each other in a duet, while Catherall sings along in the background.

artiest/joao-da-bahiana.text:
João da Bahiana, usually spelled João da Baiana, was a Brazilian percussionist and samba musician from Rio de Janeiro. He played the pandeiro, the Brazilian tambourine that plays a leading role in samba. He belonged to the old guard of carioca samba, the generation that shaped the genre at the beginning of the twentieth century, and his name is often mentioned together with that of Pixinguinha.

On record he can be heard on Macumba from 1955 and Gente da antiga from 1968, an album on which older masters of samba play together, among others. His importance lies in preserving the rhythm and atmosphere of early samba.
artiest/joao-da-bahiana.listen: Listen to a samba with pandeiro and notice how the small hand drum carries the rhythm, with short, tight strokes that both keep the beat and embellish it.

artiest/joao-gilberto.text: The singer and guitarist João Gilberto came from Juazeiro in north-eastern Brazil. In the 1950s he spent years in Rio searching for a style of his own. He found a guitar pattern that sums up the whole percussion section of the samba, and sang softly and precisely, without vibrato. In 1958 he played guitar on Chega de Saudade by Elizeth Cardoso and recorded the song himself; his album Chega de Saudade (1959) is regarded as the beginning of bossa nova. In 1963 he made Getz/Gilberto with Stan Getz. He was known as a perfectionist and rarely performed. He died in 2019.
artiest/joao-gilberto.listen: Listen to the guitar and the voice: soft, precise and just slightly apart from each other.

artiest/joaquim-callado.text:
Joaquim Antônio da Silva Callado Júnior was a Brazilian composer and flautist, born in Rio de Janeiro in 1848, where he also died in 1880. He is regarded as one of the creators of the choro, a style of Brazilian urban music that arose in the nineteenth century. His name is also spelled with one l, Calado.

His group, O Choro do Callado, played with an ebony flute, two guitars and a cavaquinho, a small guitar-like instrument. The band was known for its ease in improvising. Callado wrote, and co-wrote, many choros, a new way of playing modinhas, lundus, waltzes and polkas. His titles show how varied that work was: Adelaide, Ai, Que Gozos, Aurora, Carnival of 1867 and Celeste.

In the history of Brazilian music he is a starting point. He showed how European dances such as the waltz and the polka acquired a form of their own in Rio, with flute, guitars and improvisation. Anyone who wants to understand Brazil's later urban music sooner or later ends up at the choro.
artiest/joaquim-callado.listen: Listen to a choro for flute, guitar and cavaquinho and notice how the flute embellishes the melody while the guitar and the cavaquinho carry the rhythm.

artiest/joaquin-rodrigo.text:
Joaquín Rodrigo was a Spanish composer and virtuoso pianist, born in Sagunto near Valencia in 1901. At the age of three he went completely blind after diphtheria. At eight he began solfège, piano and violin, and from sixteen harmony and composition. He wrote his music in braille, after which it was transcribed. He studied in Valencia and with Paul Dukas in Paris, where he later studied musicology with Maurice Emmanuel and André Pirro. His first published work dates from 1923.

His most famous piece is the Concierto de Aranjuez, written in Paris in 1939 for the guitarist Regino Sainz de la Maza. It is a concerto for guitar and orchestra and a cornerstone of the classical guitar repertoire. Later he and his wife Victoria said that the piece was a response to the miscarriage of their first child. The slow movement was arranged in 1960 by the arranger Gil Evans for Miles Davis's album Sketches of Spain. The jazz guitarist Jim Hall also arranged the second movement.

The success brought commissions from top soloists. Rodrigo wrote Fantasía para un gentilhombre in 1954 for Andrés Segovia, the Concierto Andaluz for four guitars for Celedonio Romero and his three sons, a harp concerto for Nicanor Zabaleta and works for James Galway and Julian Lloyd Webber. Aranjuez and Fantasía are often paired on one record. Rodrigo died in 1999. His work shows how classical music and jazz could meet through a single melody.
artiest/joaquin-rodrigo.listen: Listen to the slow movement of the Concierto de Aranjuez and then compare it with Sketches of Spain by Miles Davis: the same melody, but in a completely different sound.

artiest/jodie-christian.text:
Jodie Christian was an American jazz pianist, known for bebop and free jazz. He was born in Chicago in 1932. His father came from Little Rock, Arkansas, from a family of sharecroppers. His grandfather sold his livestock and sent the family to Chicago to escape that life. Christian attended Wendell Phillips High School.

In Chicago he was one of the founders of the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians, the AACM, together with pianist Muhal Richard Abrams, drummer Steve McCall and composer Phil Cohran. With Abrams he also played in the Experimental Band. The AACM became an important collective for innovative Black music from the city. Christian worked at the club Jazz Showcase in Chicago and played with Eddie Harris, Stan Getz, Dexter Gordon, Gene Ammons, Roscoe Mitchell, Buddy Montgomery, Judy Roberts and John Klemmer.

As a bandleader he made a number of albums, including Blues Holiday, Rain or Shine, Front Line and, in the 1990s, Soul Fountain. He died in Chicago in 2012, at the age of eighty. His importance lies in his role as a link between bebop and the experimental jazz of his city. He played with the old guard and at the same time helped build the new form.
artiest/jodie-christian.listen: Listen to an album by Jodie Christian such as Front Line and notice how, in a blues or bebop piece, he leaves room in his solo for free, unexpected turns.

artiest/joe-cocker.text:
Joe Cocker was an English singer, known for his rough, bluesy voice and his frenzied performances, in which he waved his arms and played air guitar. He was born in Sheffield in 1944. His idols were Ray Charles and Lonnie Donegan. At twelve he sang in front of an audience for the first time, at a gig by his brother's skiffle group. With his first groups he played mainly in pubs, and in 1963 he supported the Rolling Stones. His first single, a recording of the Beatles' I'll Cry Instead, flopped in 1964.

In 1966 he formed the Grease Band with Chris Stainton. In 1968 he broke through with a new arrangement of the Beatles' With a Little Help from My Friends, with Jimmy Page on guitar. The song reached number one in the United Kingdom. In 1969 he played at Woodstock and at the Isle of Wight Festival. His second album, Joe Cocker!, included Delta Lady. The big Mad Dogs and Englishmen tour followed, with Leon Russell and more than twenty musicians, with The Letter as his first American top ten hit. Later came Unchain My Heart in 1987, among others.

Many of his best-known songs were covers of other people's songs, such as Feelin' Alright. In 2008 Cocker received an OBE and he was on Rolling Stone's list of the hundred greatest singers. He died in 2014. He showed that a singer with a rough voice can make a familiar song sound completely different.
artiest/joe-cocker.listen: Listen to With a Little Help from My Friends and notice how Cocker turns the cheerful Beatles song into a slow, screaming soul ballad.

artiest/joe-farrell.text:
Joe Farrell was an American jazz multi-instrumentalist, mainly on saxophone and flute. He was born in Chicago Heights in 1937 as Joseph Carl Firrantello. As a child he played flute and clarinet. After his studies in Urbana, in 1959, he moved to New York to work as a freelancer. He played in Ralph Marterie's band, with Maynard Ferguson and in the orchestra of Thad Jones and Mel Lewis, and recorded with Charles Mingus, Andrew Hill, Jaki Byard and Elvin Jones. After John Coltrane's death, Elvin Jones formed a trio without piano with Jimmy Garrison and Farrell.

From the late 1960s and through the 1970s he played with Chick Corea and Return to Forever. He plays flute on the first recording of Spain, a jazz standard by Corea. His best-known records under his own name appeared on the label CTI. He also played on many sessions. He played a flute solo on Aretha Franklin's Until You Come Back to Me from 1973 and on the Santana song When I Look into Your Eyes. In 1976 he made the duo album Benson and Farrell with George Benson, and in 1979 Flute Talk with Sam Most, billed as a duet between the two best jazz flautists in the world.

His last recordings are on Three-Way Mirror from 1987, with Airto and Flora Purim. Farrell died in 1986. He showed that the flute can be a full solo voice in jazz and fusion, and that a jazz player also had a role in soul and Latin music.
artiest/joe-farrell.listen: Listen to Spain by Chick Corea and Return to Forever and notice Farrell's flute, which floats light and fast above the Latin rhythm.

artiest/joe-guy.text:
Joe Guy was an American jazz trumpeter, born in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1920. He began as a young, forward-looking bebop musician and played with more important names, until a drug addiction brought his career to a halt. Much of his early life is unclear. It is known that he began his career in New York and played in Fats Waller's backing band in the late 1930s.

In 1938 he succeeded Dizzy Gillespie in Teddy Hill's orchestra and modelled his playing on that of his predecessor. In 1941 and 1942 he played regularly in the after-hours band at Minton's Playhouse, together with Nick Fenton, Kenny Clarke and Thelonious Monk. There, in jam sessions, the first forms of bebop emerged. In that period he also took part in recordings by Jerry Newman and played on tracks by Charlie Christian.

Guy struggled with a heroin addiction for most of his short career. In 1945 and 1946 he was connected with Billie Holiday both professionally and personally. When they were both arrested for drug possession, they broke with each other. He then returned to Birmingham and withdrew from music. He died in 1962, at the age of forty-one. Guy is above all an example of the young players who helped shape bebop at Minton's.
artiest/joe-guy.listen: Listen to a recording from Minton's Playhouse from 1941 or 1942 and notice how loosely and quickly the soloists play, without an arrangement, as in a jam session.

artiest/joe-henderson.text:
Joe Henderson was an American jazz tenor saxophonist and occasional flautist, born in Lima, Ohio, in 1937, one of fourteen children. His greatest inspiration was Charlie Parker. At eighteen he was already playing on the Detroit jazz scene and studying with Larry Teal. From 1960 to 1962 he was in the United States Army, after which he moved to New York. Trumpeter Kenny Dorham became his mentor.

From 1963 to 1968 he appeared on almost thirty Blue Note albums, including five under his own name. These ranged from conservative hard bop, such as Page One from 1963, to more exploratory sessions such as Inner Urge and Mode for Joe. He played an important solo on Song for My Father by Horace Silver, in whose band he played, and played on records by Lee Morgan, Grant Green and Herbie Hancock. In 1967 he signed with Milestone Records. There he experimented with jazz-funk, overdubs and electronic effects, and titles such as Power to the People and In Pursuit of Blackness showed his political awareness.

In 1971 he moved to San Francisco, where he lived for the rest of his life. In the 1980s he mainly reworked standards and his own compositions. The two-volume State of the Tenor from 1986 was recorded at the Village Vanguard. In 1991 he signed with Verve and later made an album of music by Billy Strayhorn. He died in 2001. His strength lay in his versatility: bebop, rhythm and blues, Latin and avant-garde all sounded in his playing.
artiest/joe-henderson.listen: Listen to Song for My Father by Horace Silver and notice Henderson's tenor solo, in which he plays bluesy and unexpected phrases over a Latin rhythm.

artiest/joe-hisaishi.text: Joe Hisaishi (born Mamoru Fujisawa in 1950) studied composition at the Kunitachi College of Music and began in minimal music. His stage name is a Japanese corruption of Quincy Jones. Beginning with Kaze no tani no Naushika (1984), he wrote the music for almost all of Hayao Miyazaki's films, such as Tonari no Totoro (1988), Mononoke-hime (1997) and Sen to Chihiro no kamikakushi (2001). His style combines simple, song-like melodies with romantic orchestral music and repeated patterns from minimal music. For director Takeshi Kitano he wrote cooler, sparer music, as in Hana-bi (1997). He often conducts his music himself in concerts.
artiest/joe-hisaishi.listen: Notice the piano melody that sounds simple at first and is then taken over by strings, with small repeated patterns underneath.

artiest/joe-morello.text:
Joe Morello was an American jazz drummer, born in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1928. He had poor eyesight from birth and therefore looked for activities indoors. He began playing the violin at six, and as a child he appeared as a soloist with the Boston Symphony Orchestra. When he heard the violinist Jascha Heifetz at fifteen, he decided he would never equal his sound. He switched to drums and studied with George Lawrence Stone, who dedicated one of his textbooks to him.

In New York, Morello played with guitarist Tal Farlow and in pianist Marian McPartland's trio, among others. He turned down offers from Benny Goodman and Tommy Dorsey and instead went on tour with the Dave Brubeck Quartet, where he stayed for more than ten years. With saxophonist Paul Desmond, bassist Eugene Wright and Brubeck he made Time Out (1959). Desmond wrote Take Five specially to showcase Morello in a time signature of five beats. He also plays in unusual time signatures on Blue Rondo à la Turk and Unsquare Dance.

Morello was a drummer with an enormous technique, who used that technique to play musically. He showed that you can swing and solo in odd time signatures. In doing so he made Brubeck's rhythmic experiments possible. In 1976 he went blind, and after that he devoted himself mainly to teaching, including Max Weinberg. He died in 2011.
artiest/joe-morello.listen: Listen to Take Five (1959) by the Dave Brubeck Quartet. Count along in five beats and notice how Morello keeps that metre going in his drum solo while the piano carries on with the same pattern.

artiest/joe-perry.text:
Joe Perry is an American guitarist, born Joseph Pereira in Lawrence, Massachusetts, in 1950. As a boy he wanted to be a marine biologist, but at a boarding school in Vermont he heard the music of Jimi Hendrix, The Who, The Kinks and The Yardbirds from his classmates. He had already learned to play guitar at ten, right-handed although he is left-handed. Now he sat in his room for hours playing riffs from records.

In the late 1960s Perry started The Jam Band with bassist Tom Hamilton. When singer Steven Tyler, guitarist Brad Whitford and drummer Joey Kramer joined, the name became Aerosmith. At first the band was dismissed as a copy of The Rolling Stones, but in the mid-1970s success came, with Dream On and the albums Toys in the Attic (1975) and Rocks (1976), with songs such as Sweet Emotion and Walk This Way. Perry and Tyler wrote most of the songs together and became known as the Toxic Twins, because of their drug use. In 1979 Perry left after a quarrel and started the Joe Perry Project. In 1984 he returned to Aerosmith.

In 1986 Perry and Tyler recorded a new version of Walk This Way with Run-DMC. That record helped rap break through to a wide audience and gave Aerosmith a second life, with albums such as Permanent Vacation (1987) and Pump (1989). Perry is known for his raw, bluesy riffs, which he took from the British rock of the 1960s.
artiest/joe-perry.listen: Listen to Walk This Way (1986) by Run-DMC with Aerosmith. Notice how Perry's guitar riff and the DJ's beat go together, and how rock and rap literally meet in the song.

artiest/joe-strummer.text:
Joe Strummer, born John Graham Mellor in Ankara in 1952, was a British musician and co-founder, lyricist, rhythm guitarist and singer of the punk band The Clash. His mother was Scottish and his father English. He loved Little Richard, the Beach Boys and Woody Guthrie. After school he studied at an art school in London, played in a band in Wales in 1973 and took his stage name in 1975. He became the singer of the 101ers.

In 1976 he saw the Sex Pistols supporting the 101ers. Shortly afterwards Bernie Rhodes and Mick Jones asked him to be their singer. He left the 101ers and, with Jones, bassist Paul Simonon and others, formed The Clash. Their lyrics were about social decay, unemployment, racism, police violence and militarism. Strummer supported Rock Against Racism and the Anti-Nazi League. London Calling was chosen by Rolling Stone as the best album of the 1980s. In 1982 he disappeared before the release of Combat Rock, and in 1983 he threw Mick Jones out of the band. In 1986 The Clash came to an end.

Afterwards he worked on films, such as Sid and Nancy and Walker, appeared in Jim Jarmusch's Mystery Train and toured with The Pogues. His 1989 solo album Earthquake Weather flopped. Later he founded the Mescaleros and presented the BBC radio programme London Calling. He died in 2002 and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with The Clash in 2003.
artiest/joe-strummer.listen: Listen to London Calling by The Clash and notice Strummer's hoarse, urgent voice and the sturdy rhythm of guitar and bass that makes the song sound almost like an alarm.

artiest/joe-walsh.text:
Joe Walsh is an American guitarist, singer and songwriter, born in Wichita, Kansas, in 1947. His father, a pilot, was killed when Walsh was two. His mother was a classically trained pianist. His stepfather gave him his surname. At ten he was given a guitar and he wanted to become a guitarist after hearing Walk Don't Run by The Ventures. He played in bands in New Jersey and Ohio and briefly attended Kent State University.

He gained national fame with the James Gang, whose hit Funk 49 showed off his playing. After leaving in 1972 he formed Barnstorm. At the suggestion of producer Bill Szymczyk he became the Eagles' guitarist and keyboardist in 1975, succeeding Bernie Leadon. His first album with the group was Hotel California. In 1998 a readers' poll by Guitarist magazine chose the solos by Walsh and Don Felder in Hotel California as the best guitar solos ever. As a solo artist he had hits with Rocky Mountain Way, Life's Been Good, All Night Long and Ordinary Average Guy.

Walsh made twelve studio albums under his own name and also played in Ringo Starr and His All-Starr Band. His guitar work is sharp and hard, but he also has a funny, playful side, as Life's Been Good shows. He showed that a rock guitarist can keep a voice of his own both in a hard rock trio and in a big West Coast band.
artiest/joe-walsh.listen: Listen to Hotel California by the Eagles and notice the two guitar solos at the end, by Walsh and Don Felder, which answer each other.

artiest/joe-zawinul.text: The keyboardist Joe Zawinul grew up in Vienna, where he learned accordion and classical piano. In 1959 he left for the United States and from 1961 he played for almost ten years with Cannonball Adderley, for whom he wrote Mercy, Mercy, Mercy, on electric piano. He wrote the title piece of In a Silent Way for Miles Davis. In 1970, with Wayne Shorter, he founded Weather Report, the best-known fusion band of the 1970s. Zawinul used synthesizers like an orchestra. Birdland (1977), a tribute to the New York jazz club, became a hit and a standard. Later he led the Zawinul Syndicate with musicians from all over the world.
artiest/joe-zawinul.listen: Listen to the synthesizers that together sound like an orchestra.

artiest/joey-dee-and-the-starliters.text:
Joey Dee and the Starliters were an American pop group from New Jersey. They are best known for Peppermint Twist from 1961, a record that sold a million copies. The best-known line-up consisted of Joey Dee, David Brigati and Larry Vernieri as singers and Carlton Lattimore on organ. Their first single, in 1958, was Lorraine, with singer Rogers Freeman. That same year Dee brought in David Brigati.

In 1960 the agent Don Davis saw the group perform in Lodi, New Jersey. He booked them at the Peppermint Lounge, a small club in New York, for what was meant to be a one-off weekend. It became the start of their success, and the club became the centre of the twist craze. In 1961 the group appeared in the film Hey, Let's Twist, a fictional story built around Dee and the Peppermint Lounge, and in 1962 in Two Tickets to Paris. A song from it, What Kind of Love Is This, written by Johnny Nash, reached the American top twenty. In 1963 Dee recorded the album Dance, Dance, Dance with the Ronettes as backing singers, and Hot Pastrami with Mashed Potatoes reached the top forty.

Jimi Hendrix and Joe Pesci also played guitar with the group in the 1960s. Dee went on making records into the 1970s and still performs. In 2010 the group was given a street corner in its home town of Passaic. The group stands for the dance craze in which a new dance could drive an entire pop culture within a few months.
artiest/joey-dee-and-the-starliters.listen: Listen to Peppermint Twist and notice how the rhythm, the cheering and the singing are made for the dance floor, so that you can almost hear the twist.

artiest/joey-tempest.text:
Joey Tempest, whose real name is Rolf Magnus Joakim Larsson, is a Swedish singer and the lead singer of the rock band Europe. He was born in Stockholm in 1963 and grew up in the suburb of Upplands Väsby. As a child he recorded songs from British and American radio on a tape recorder. His biggest influences were Thin Lizzy and Led Zeppelin. In 1979 he came up with his stage name, inspired by Shakespeare's The Tempest and by the song Sparks of the Tempest by the group Kansas.

He formed the band Force with guitarist John Norum, bassist Peter Olsson and drummer Tony Reno, which later became Europe. Tempest wrote most of Europe's hits, such as The Final Countdown, Rock the Night, Cherokee, Open Your Heart and Carrie. The Final Countdown topped the sales charts in 26 countries and was played at the closing of the 1988 Olympic Games. Out of This World followed in 1988, and Prisoners in Paradise.

After the band's hiatus he began a solo career. In 1995 his debut A Place to Call Home appeared, a singer-songwriter album that he himself described as influenced by Van Morrison and Bob Dylan. Azalea Place followed in 1997 and Joey Tempest in 2002. Almost twelve years after the break-up, Europe returned in 2004 with the same line-up, with Start from the Dark. Tempest stands for the Scandinavian hard rock of the 1980s, in which a huge synthesizer theme and staying power came together.
artiest/joey-tempest.listen: Listen to The Final Countdown and notice the synthesizer theme with which the song begins and which keeps returning, with the solid rock guitars underneath.

artiest/johann-johannsson.text: Jóhann Jóhannsson was born in Reykjavík in 1969. He was not a classically trained composer but came from indie rock and experimental electronic music. He forged orchestra, choir and electronic processing into a single field of sound. With director Denis Villeneuve he made Prisoners (2013), Sicario (2015) and Arrival (2016). In Sicario a rumbling, low rhythm sounds like approaching danger. In Arrival he processed voices so that they sound like an alien language. His score for The Theory of Everything (2014), by contrast, is light and warm and won a Golden Globe. He died in Berlin in 2018, aged 48. Hildur Guðnadóttir worked closely with him.
artiest/johann-johannsson.listen: Notice the low rumble and the processed voices: the boundary between music and sound design disappears.

artiest/johann-nepomuk-hummel.text:
Johann Nepomuk Hummel was an Austrian composer and pianist, born in Pressburg, present-day Bratislava, in 1778. His father was a violinist and music teacher. He was a child prodigy. When he was eight, Mozart offered him lessons, and he lived in Mozart's house for two years, free of charge. At nine he played for the first time at a Mozart concert. He then toured Europe with his father. In London he was taught by Muzio Clementi and played with great success. In 1791, at the age of thirteen, he gave the premiere of a Haydn piano trio.

In Vienna he studied with Johann Georg Albrechtsberger, Joseph Haydn and Antonio Salieri. There he became friends with the young Ludwig van Beethoven, who studied with the same teachers. He often visited Beethoven later and played at his memorial concert. In 1813 he married the opera singer Elisabeth Röckel, with whom he toured Russia and the rest of Europe the following year.

His music stands at the transition from the Classical to the Romantic period. He wrote piano concertos, trios and quintets, and concertos for trumpet, bassoon and oboe, among other works. His trumpet concerto in particular is frequently recorded. He had a great influence on later pianists. Hummel died in 1837. His work shows how the elegance of Mozart and Haydn passed into the virtuosity of the nineteenth century.
artiest/johann-nepomuk-hummel.listen: Listen to Hummel's trumpet concerto and notice how the soloist begins with a short, fanfare-like theme that is then developed ever more ornately.

artiest/johann-pachelbel.text:
Johann Pachelbel was a German Baroque composer, organist and music teacher. He was baptised in Nuremberg in 1653, the son of a wine merchant. From an early age he stood out for his musical and scholastic talent. After studies in Altdorf and Regensburg he worked as an organist in Vienna, Eisenach, Erfurt, Stuttgart and Gotha, and finally back in his home town, where he died in 1706.

In his own day Pachelbel was known mainly as an organist and as a composer of Protestant church music. He wrote chorale preludes, fugues, variations for harpsichord and chamber music. His style was clear and orderly, with highly singable melodies. He had many pupils and his work became a model for composers in southern and central Germany. In Erfurt he taught Johann Christoph Bach, the elder brother and later teacher of Johann Sebastian Bach.

Today everyone knows him for one piece: the Canon in D, in full Canon and Gigue for three violins and basso continuo. When he wrote it is not certain. The piece is a canon, in which the violins follow one another with the same melody, above a bass line that is repeated over and over. In the twentieth century it became enormously popular. The chord sequence that goes with that bass line has since turned up in countless pop songs. In this way a Baroque composer lives on in the hit parade.
artiest/johann-pachelbel.listen: Listen to the Canon in D and first follow only the bass, which keeps repeating the same eight notes. Then notice how the violins enter one by one with the same melody, each following the one before.

artiest/johann-sebastian-bach.text: Johann Sebastian Bach worked as an organist and Kapellmeister in Arnstadt, Weimar and Köthen, among other places, and from 1723 as cantor of the Thomaskirche in Leipzig. He forged the Italian concerto, the French dance and the German chorale into a counterpoint of unrivalled richness. His Matthäus-Passion (St Matthew Passion) from 1727 tells the story of the Passion with two choirs and two orchestras. After his death that work fell into oblivion, until Felix Mendelssohn performed it again in 1829.
artiest/johann-sebastian-bach.listen: Listen to the solo violin at the beginning of Erbarme dich and hear how the long, plaintive melody already anticipates what the alto voice is about to sing.

artiest/johann-strauss-ii.text: Johann Strauss the Younger founded his own dance orchestra in Vienna in 1844 and, like his father, became known as the Waltz King. He wrote hundreds of dances and turned the waltz into an extended concert form, with an introduction, a series of waltzes and a coda. An der schönen blauen Donau from 1867 grew into an unofficial national anthem of Austria. With Die Fledermaus from 1874 he wrote the best-known Viennese operetta.
artiest/johann-strauss-ii.listen: Listen to the beginning of An der schönen blauen Donau and hear how the long introduction with tremolo strings slowly works towards the first waltz.

artiest/johannes-brahms.text: Johannes Brahms came from Hamburg, was announced by Robert Schumann at the age of twenty as the new master, and later settled in Vienna. He remained faithful to classical forms such as the symphony, the sonata and the variation, and was thus regarded as the counterpart to Wagner and Liszt. His Ein deutsches Requiem from 1868 uses not the Latin Mass for the dead but German Bible texts that comfort the bereaved. Clara Schumann remained his most important friend and adviser throughout his life.
artiest/johannes-brahms.listen: Listen to Denn alles Fleisch and hear how the choir sings softly and heavily above a slow funeral march with timpani.

artiest/johannes-kalitzke.text:
Johannes Kalitzke is a German composer and conductor, born in Cologne in 1959. He had piano lessons from 1967 to 1977, studied church music from 1974 to 1976 and then at the Musikhochschule Köln, with piano under Aloys Kontarsky, conducting under Wolfgang von der Nahmer and composition under York Höller, among others. Later he worked at IRCAM in Paris.

From 1984 to 1990 he was first Kapellmeister and then chief conductor at the Musiktheater im Revier in Gelsenkirchen, and from 1986 director of the Forum für Neue Musik. From 1991 he was artistic director of the ensemble musikFabrik. Since 1996 he has taught at the Darmstädter Ferienkurse, and since 2015 he has been professor of conducting contemporary music at the Mozarteum in Salzburg.

He wrote five operas. The first, Bericht über den Tod des Musikers Jack Tiergarten, premiered in 1996 at the Munich Biennale. Molière oder die Henker der Komödianten followed in 1998 and Inferno in 2004. His fifth opera, Pym, based on the novel by Edgar Allan Poe, premiered in Heidelberg in 2016. There are also recordings of his orchestral works, symphonies and chamber music, and of Lost Highway, based on the film by David Lynch. Kalitzke stands for contemporary art music in Germany, as a writer and as a conductor who makes new works performable.
artiest/johannes-kalitzke.listen: Listen to an excerpt by Kalitzke and notice the way the orchestra and the soloists set unexpected, sharp tone colours side by side.

artiest/johannes-ockeghem.text:
Johannes Ockeghem was a Franco-Flemish composer and singer of the early Renaissance. He was born around 1410, possibly in Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut, but the year is uncertain and estimates run as late as 1430. Like many composers of his time he began as a choirboy. For most of his career he served the French royal chapel, under Charles VII, Louis XI and Charles VIII.

In the period between Guillaume Du Fay and Josquin des Prez he was the leading European composer. Together with Antoine Busnois he was one of the great names of the second half of the fifteenth century. Probably only part of his work has survived: about fourteen Masses, twenty chansons and fewer than ten motets. The well-known pieces include the Missa prolationum, which is built on canons, and the Missa cuiusvis toni, as well as his Requiem.

Ockeghem died in 1497. Many poets and musicians mourned his death, among them Erasmus, Guillaume Crétin, Jean Molinet and Josquin, who wrote the famous lament Nymphes des bois for him. To a modern ear his music is full of long, almost endless lines, with voices moving fluidly through one another. He shows how the sung polyphonic music of the late Middle Ages developed into the polyphony of the Renaissance.
artiest/johannes-ockeghem.listen: Listen to the Missa prolationum and notice how the voices sing the same melody at different speeds at the same time, creating a rich, swaying polyphony.
